title: Oversmoothing, "Oversquashing'', Heterophily, Long-Range, and more: Demystifying Common Beliefs in Graph Machine Learning
claim: Whether signals vanish or explode with depth depends on the architecture and the weight scale, so common beliefs about universal behavior fail.
layout: 4 line-plot panels in a row, shared depth axis, log y-scale
description: A single row of four log-scale line plots with depth (number of layers, from 1 to 64) on the x-axis. Panels (a) and (b) show Dirichlet Energy (solid lines) and feature norm (dashed lines) for four graph neural network architectures: GCN in dark blue, GAT in light green, SAGE in teal, and GIN in orange. Panels (c) and (d) show the RQ metric for the same four architectures. The first panel in each pair uses weight W and the second uses 2W. Shaded bands show variability across 50 random seeds on Cora. The eye goes first to the orange GIN curve, which shoots up by many orders of magnitude. In the W panels the other curves decay with depth. In the 2W panels they grow. Short captions under each panel label the setting.
caption: (a-b): We depict the evolution, with increasing number of layers, of the DE, using W and 2W feature transformations for different architectures. (c-d): Evolution of the RQ for W and 2W as before. Experiments run on the Cora dataset for 50 random seeds. A larger version for better visualization is available in Fig. 8.
abstract: After a renaissance phase in which researchers revisited the message-passing paradigm through the lens of deep learning, the graph machine learning community shifted its attention towards a deeper and practical understanding of message-passing's benefits and limitations. In this paper, we notice how the fast pace of progress around the topics of oversmoothing and oversquashing, the homophily-heterophily dichotomy, and long-range tasks, came with the consolidation of commonly accepted beliefs and assumptions -- under the form of universal statements -- that are not always true nor easy to distinguish from each other. We argue that this has led to ambiguities around the investigated problems, preventing researchers from focusing on and addressing precise research questions while causing a good amount of misunderstandings. Our contribution is to make such common beliefs explicit and encourage critical thinking around these topics, refuting universal statements via simple yet formally sufficient counterexamples. The end goal is to clarify conceptual differences, helping researchers address more clearly defined and targeted problems.
